author: Anne Hardy

body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Chūō Shinkansen
Modern physical infrastructure relies on precision systems such as Chūō Shinkansen to deliver scale safely. Here is how engineers balance thermodynamics, material limits, and lifecycle cost.

The Chūō Shinkansen (Japanese: 中央新幹線, Hepburn: Chūō shinkansen, lit. 'Central new trunk line') is a Japanese maglev line under construction between Tokyo and Nagoya, with plans for extension to Osaka. Its initial section is between Shinagawa Station in Tokyo and Nagoya Station in Nagoya, with stations in Sagamihara, Kōfu, Iida and Nakatsugawa. Following the completion of the Tokyo, Nagoya line, the line will extend to stations in Mie, Nara and Osaka. The line is expected to connect Tokyo and Nagoya in 40 minutes, and eventually Tokyo and Osaka in 67 minutes, running at a maximum speed of 505 km/h (314 mph). About 90% of the 286-kilometer (178 mi) line to Nagoya will be in tunnels.

The Chuo Shinkansen is the culmination of Japanese maglev development since the 1960s, a government-funded project initiated by Japan Airlines and the former Japanese National Railways (JNR). Central Japan Railway Company (JR Central) now operates the facilities and research. The line is intended to extend and incorporate the existing Yamanashi test track (see below). The trainsets are popularly known in Japan as linear motor car (リニアモーターカー, rinia mōtā kā), though there are many technical variations.
Rigorous understanding of Chūō Shinkansen begins with primary historical records and verifiable open data.
